title: Core ideas in psychology
description: How people learn, remember, grow up and sway one another, and who found it out.

ideas.title: Learning by association and consequence
ideas.summary: Behavior is shaped by pairing signals with events (classical conditioning) and by what follows an action (operant).

items.q: Which Russian physiologist discovered classical conditioning while studying digestion in dogs?
items.a: Ivan Pavlov

items.q: What is classical conditioning?
items.a: Learning to respond to a neutral signal because it has been paired with something that naturally triggers the response

items.q: What is operant conditioning, the kind of learning studied by B. F. Skinner?
items.a: Learning in which a behavior is strengthened or weakened by its consequences

items.q: In operant conditioning, what is negative reinforcement?
items.a: Strengthening a behavior by taking away something unpleasant; it is not punishment

items.q: A dog gets a treat each time it sits on command, and soon sits more often. Which kind of conditioning is this?
items.a: Operant conditioning (positive reinforcement)

items.q: Which schedule of reinforcement, the one slot machines use, makes a behavior hardest to extinguish?
items.a: A variable-ratio schedule: reward after an unpredictable number of responses

ideas.title: How memory works
ideas.summary: Memory is encoded, stored and retrieved; it fades along a curve, and it is rebuilt rather than replayed when we recall.

items.q: What are the three stages of memory processing, in order?
items.a: Encoding, storage, retrieval

items.q: Which German psychologist first measured the forgetting curve, in the 1880s?
items.a: Hermann Ebbinghaus

items.q: In the psychology of memory, what is the spacing effect?
items.a: Material is remembered better when study is spread out over time than when it is crammed

items.q: What is the testing effect, also called retrieval practice?
items.a: Recalling something from memory strengthens it more than rereading it does

items.q: What did George Miller's 1956 paper give as the capacity of short-term memory?
items.a: About seven items, plus or minus two

items.q: What did Elizabeth Loftus's misinformation experiments show about eyewitness memory?
items.a: Memories can be altered by leading questions and by information received after the event

ideas.title: How children develop
ideas.summary: Children's thinking and attachments develop in recognizable steps, charted by Piaget, Vygotsky and Bowlby.

items.q: Which Swiss psychologist proposed that children's thinking develops through four stages, from sensorimotor to formal operational?
items.a: Jean Piaget

items.q: In Piaget's theory of child development, what is object permanence?
items.a: Understanding that things continue to exist when they are out of sight

items.q: What is Vygotsky's zone of proximal development?
items.a: The range of tasks a learner can do with help but cannot yet do alone

items.q: What does attachment theory, developed by John Bowlby, claim?
items.a: An infant's early bond with a caregiver shapes later emotional and social development

ideas.title: Social influence
ideas.summary: Ordinary people conform, obey and stand by far more than they expect to, as classic experiments showed.

items.q: What did Solomon Asch's line-judging experiments of the 1950s demonstrate?
items.a: Conformity: people often go along with a group's plainly wrong answer

items.q: What did Stanley Milgram's shock experiments of the early 1960s show about obedience?
items.a: Many ordinary people will obey an authority even when told to give seemingly painful electric shocks

items.q: In social psychology, what is the bystander effect?
items.a: An individual may be less likely to help when others are present than when alone

items.q: What is cognitive dissonance, the theory proposed by Leon Festinger?
items.a: The discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs, or acting against a belief, which we ease by changing one of them

ideas.title: Personality and motivation
ideas.summary: Trait psychology describes personality along five broad dimensions, and theories of motivation ask what moves us to act.

items.q: In the Big Five model of personality, which trait is the tendency to feel negative emotions such as anxiety?
items.a: Neuroticism

items.q: Which Big Five personality trait describes being organized, dependable and self-disciplined?
items.a: Conscientiousness

items.q: In Maslow's classic hierarchy of needs, which need sits at the top?
items.a: Self-actualization

items.q: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation?
items.a: Intrinsic: doing something for its own sake; extrinsic: doing it for an outside reward or to avoid a penalty
